scope: All 75 active entries match validated build inputs; 75 earlier entries are preserved exactly, and 1 superseded entry is preserved byte-for-byte in the archive. Matching filenames, source order, scoped references, unique IDs, coverage lists, folder pairing and ZIP byte equality checked. Source hashes are verified for collections and in the lesson module index. Numeric answers and accept variants are checked in the referenced lesson validation reports. Archived checks are excluded from active totals.
limitations: Human educational review required; all cards are drafts.
Reference controller verified; script-agent integration not tested.
Grade 2 Module 1 remains one combined concept card for Lessons 1–8.
Human educational review remains required; script-agent integration is not tested.
Easy is one reused practice calculation. Some source lessons have no simpler core practice item and require several place value actions to finish it.
Numeric answers assess use of strategies; explanations of why a method is faster are modeled in guidance but not scored as spoken reasoning.

Lesson 11 exp_1 incorrectly says the tens total in 342 + 169 is 10; the correct total including the new ten is 11. New generated items cite exp_2, exp_3 and ex_1; the reused easy answer uses corrected arithmetic. Original concept JSON is preserved.
Source metadata and worksheet numbering remain draft uncertainties.
Lessons 18–20 reuse open questions. Grade equivalent explanations against the linked rubric, using partial only when its stated criterion is met.
Generated parity questions use numeric codes with explicit labels. These codes represent even/odd judgments rather than object counts.
Lesson 12 is about constructing equal squares, shared lines and spatial structuring. These actions are prompted and explained, but numeric answers do not validate the actual drawing.
Source metadata and pictured worksheet uncertainties remain in the linked concept cards.
Lessons 1–4 prompt sorting, tallies and graph construction, but numeric answers do not verify the actual tables, labels, scales or drawings.
Lesson 5 answers count coins rather than their value in cents. Lessons 6–9 use the source US coin and dollar denominations.
Lesson 9 numeric totals and worked solutions model fair trades; accepting a total alone cannot verify a learner performed the trade.
Lesson 10 asks for the minimum coin count; the answer does not itself verify the learner selected the shown combination.
Source easy items are the simplest numeric practice items available; Lesson 7 needs skip-counting two coin types and Lesson 9 easy checks counting as a prerequisite to equivalent combinations.
Generated shape/fraction naming questions use explicitly stated numeric choice keys. A correct code does not verify spoken mathematical vocabulary or a learner explanation.
Drawings, folds, joins and matching actions are described and modelled; numeric responses do not verify that the learner actually constructed or checked them.
The source defines trapezoid inclusively as at least one parallel side pair. The square question asks for the most specific name among the listed choices.
Lesson 2 easy combines quadrilateral recognition with finding missing sides; Lesson 4 easy counts index-card angles as a prerequisite for square-corner classification.
Source geometry specifications, metadata and pictured worksheet uncertainties remain in linked concept cards.
Human educational review and script-agent integration remain outstanding.
Lesson objectives and asset scopes are adapted from the combined concept, without consulting the unavailable original lesson PDFs. Source metadata and worksheet uncertainties remain.
Shared original support hints retain their source provenance; those generic hints do not authorize importing another lesson's explanations or assessment methods.

Lesson 1 has a finite set of ten/teen facts, so fixed facts can recur in new situations. Hard work includes counting ones, forming and naming a ten-and-ones number, then checking in the opposite order.
Source open questions retain their original semantic rubrics and require semantic grading; they are not converted into exact-answer questions.
